title: Use possible futures to understand the present
original: What we are interested in, though, is the idea of possible futures and using them as tools to better understand the present and to discuss the kind of future people want, and, of course, ones people do not want.
meaning: A possible future helps people examine present choices and discuss how they want to live.
application: A imagines a museum work continuing through personal-item patterns. B imagines a museum displaying postcards that grow through conversations. The possible futures help visitors examine their own interaction.

title: A future is a medium for thinking
original: For us futures are not a destination or something to be strived for but a medium to aid imaginative thought—to speculate with.
meaning: A possible future lets people think about a way of living and decide what they want to keep or change.
application: After the ordinary activity, introduce a future museum arrangement. Ask what it would change and what visitors would keep, alter or refuse. This discussion connects the small AI task to choices about museum life.

title: A prop makes another possibility discussable
original: They help us think about alternative possibilities—they challenge the ideals, values, and beliefs of our society embodied in material culture.
meaning: The object supports reflection on the values embodied in a possible arrangement.
application: A uses its local-item previews and a future label. B uses the draft, reply and final postcard. Each small prop gives people something concrete to point to when they discuss a museum’s choices.

title: A prop can actually work
original: For some, the term prop means a fake object, something that doesn’t work, but in the context of a speculative design, a prop can be a fully working prototype or not.
meaning: A working prototype can serve as a prop for an imagined situation. Its role is to make that situation available for discussion.
application: Run the actual image and translation functions during the study. Use their outputs as props for the later, clearly introduced future scenario.

title: Leave space for people’s own interpretations
original: Prefigurative futures (or pre-enactments?) also use props to transport viewers’ imagination but, whereas in this role they are bringing a specific future to the present so that it can be partially experienced in advance, user-tested, or prepared for, we are more interested in using props to transport viewers’ imagination into a thought experiment, or what-if, and allow enough room for them to make their own interpretations.
meaning: Participants can give their own answers to an imagined situation. The researcher should leave those answers open.
application: Visitors can accept, alter or stop an AI preview. They can keep different interpretations after understanding one another. Their choices shape the discussion.

title: People may make their own judgments
original: We view people as free agents, not necessarily rational, but free to make up their own minds.
meaning: This is a commitment to participants’ freedom to judge and choose.
application: People can choose the AI route, a prepared input, a plain card and their receipt method. Pilot sessions reveal which routes need further support.

title: Create a space for discussion
original: This form of design thrives on imagination and aims to open up new perspectives on what are sometimes called wicked problems, to create spaces for discussion and debate about alternative ways of being, and to inspire and encourage people’s imaginations to flow freely.
meaning: Speculation opens a discussion about how life could be different. A feature test needs this wider question to become part of that discussion.
application: A discusses how personal use carries a work forward. B discusses how a museum can show a meaning that developed between people. Both invite alternative answers.

title: An alternative must open a gap with the present
original: It is the gap between reality as we know it and the different idea of reality referred to in the critical design proposal that creates the space for discussion.
meaning: A proposal opens discussion by making another arrangement available. Its fictional rule gives participants a concrete alternative to compare with their present experience.
application: For each probe, explain the current activity, the future museum rule, the prop that makes it visible and the choice left to participants. This sequence explains why we select and revise a direction.

title: The Statistical Clock · reasoning for Probe 01
original: What would have to change for a need like this to emerge?
creator: Dunne & Raby with Michael Anastassiades
case_description: The Statistical Clock is an imagined household clock that reports deaths in different kinds of transport. It takes information people may avoid and puts it into an ordinary daily object. The designers ask what kind of life would make someone want this clock. The clock helps people discuss that life.
meaning: Put a familiar rule into a small, visible object so people can discuss how that rule shapes daily life. The clock makes daily reminders visible. Probe 1 can make the rule “AI speaks first” visible through a small museum display card. The question then concerns how that rule shapes the start of a visit.
application: After the normal question task, place the AI answer at the top of a clearly imagined museum display card. Put the visitor’s own explanation beside it. Ask what changes when the AI version always goes first. Keep 1 as a short introduction. A future standalone version could focus on who sets the starting point of interpretation.

title: The Islanders · reasoning for Probe 02
original: It is the emphasis on transporting the imagination that distinguishes them from other object types including products, prototypes, and models.
creator: Charles Avery, discussed by Dunne & Raby
case_description: In Charles Avery’s The Islanders, drawings, objects, models and found bones appear to come from a traveller’s visit to an invented island. Viewers use these small clues to imagine a larger place and its way of life. A small physical thing can therefore help someone think about an imagined world.
meaning: A small object can help people imagine the larger world in which it belongs. The island’s objects make an invented place imaginable. A uses the cuff or bag preview and a future museum label to suggest a museum where heritage patterns keep entering everyday belongings.
application: Complete A’s two local captures. Show the two actual previews beside a fictional label saying “Each version continues the original work”. Ask what kind of connection the wearable or everyday version carries forward. Develop A around the local material action and its two visual responses. The future label helps visitors connect their experience with a wider question about how a museum work can continue through personal use.

title: Plant Fiction · reasoning for Probe 03
original: There is a very important difference between inviting viewers to “make-believe” and asking them to “believe.”
creator: Troika, discussed by Dunne & Raby
case_description: Troika’s Plant Fiction presents invented plants with plausible images and short texts about how they might be used in a near-future London. The plants belong to a made-up situation. The project tells viewers that it is fiction, so they can explore the situation without being told a false discovery has occurred. One example, Selfeater, is imagined to break down its own material to help make fuel. Its picture and short story let viewers think about that future use.
meaning: Give an imagined image a clear setting and purpose, so viewers can explore the proposed future. Plant Fiction explains what its invented plants would do in future London. Probe 3 needs an equally clear purpose for its changed pattern. Adapting one detail to a cuff or bag gives the change a concrete everyday use.
application: Show the source, one local-item adaptation and a short label describing its imagined use. Ask which source detail the person wants to carry into that use and why. Keep 3 as a possible focused variant. A already uses a local item and visual changes. A separate Probe 3 would need its own use or research question.

title: United Micro Kingdoms · reasoning for Probe 04
original: Each vehicle would embody different ideologies, values, priorities, and belief systems—essentially alternative worldviews.
creator: Dunne & Raby
case_description: United Micro Kingdoms imagines several different societies and designs a vehicle for each one. Each vehicle shows choices about how people travel and live together. Looking at them helps viewers compare what each society makes easier and what it gives up. The pictured Digicars belong to a made-up society where software manages travel and road prices. The Biocar belongs to a society built around biotechnology. These two images show how different choices can shape everyday travel.
meaning: Make different choices visible through objects people can compare. The vehicles show different ways of organising travel and everyday life. B’s first draft, reply and final postcard show choices about whose interpretation becomes visible. The same card makes those choices easy to point to.
application: Keep the draft postcard, the real reply and the final postcard together. After the exchange, use a fictional museum display label and ask whether visitors should see the final postcard alone or the conversation that shaped it. Combine 4 and 5 as B. Keep the conversation visible and use its related postcard as a concrete prop for discussing interpretation and display. Round 1 begins with a local message area and prepared-image cards.

title: Huggable Atomic Mushrooms · reasoning for Probe 05
original: It is through its demeanor that one starts to wonder just how serious it is.
creator: Dunne & Raby with Michael Anastassiades
case_description: Huggable Atomic Mushrooms are soft objects shaped like clouds from nuclear tests. Their friendly feel sits beside a frightening subject. This makes viewers ask why an inviting object presents that subject in this way. Their meaning comes from this relationship between form and subject.
meaning: The way an object looks and feels can change how its subject is understood. The soft mushroom form changes how viewers meet the subject of nuclear tests. In B, a friendly pattern preview can also change the tone of a personal account. The recipient’s real response shows what the draft conveyed.
application: Let the recipient respond to the first postcard, including its image. The sender then keeps or clarifies its words and picture on the same card. Ask which version expresses the intended connection to the object. Combine 4 and 5 as B. Keep the conversation visible and use its related postcard as a concrete prop for discussing interpretation and display. Round 1 begins with a local message area and prepared-image cards.
